claim: Heterotrimeric G-proteins are signal transducers involved in mediating the action of many natural extracellular stimuli and many therapeutic agents.
source: Heterotrimeric G-proteins are signal transducers involved in mediating the action of many natural extracellular stimuli and many therapeutic agents.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about G-proteins.

claim: LOV2GIVe is an engineered modular protein that allows the activation of heterotrimeric G-proteins with blue light.
source: Here, we developed LOV2GIVe, an engineered modular protein that allows the activation of heterotrimeric G-proteins with blue light.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the manuscript, supported by multiple experimental results shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: LOV2GIVe consists of the fusion of a G-protein activating peptide derived from a non-GPCR regulator of G-proteins to a small plant protein domain.
source: Instead, LOV2GIVe consists of the fusion of a G-protein activating peptide derived from a non-GPCR regulator of G-proteins to a small plant protein domain, such that light uncages the G-protein activating module.
evidence: This describes the design principle of LOV2GIVe, which is demonstrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Targeting LOV2GIVe to cell membranes allowed for light-dependent activation of Gi proteins in different experimental systems.
source: Targeting LOV2GIVe to cell membranes allowed for light-dependent activation of Gi proteins in different experimental systems.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: GPCRs are Guanine nucleotide Exchange Factors (GEFs) that activate G-proteins by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP on the Gα-subunits.
source: GPCRs are Guanine nucleotide Exchange Factors (GEFs) that activate G-proteins by promoting the exchange of GDP for GTP on the Gα-subunits (Gilman, 1987).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to established literature.

claim: More than 30% of drugs on the market target the GPCR-G-protein signaling axis.
source: This signaling axis regulates a myriad of (patho)physiological processes and also represents the target for >30% of drugs on the market (Sriram and Insel, 2018), which fuels the interest in developing tools to manipulate G-protein activity in cells with high precision.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Metazoan opsins are light-activated GPCRs that have been repurposed as optogenetic tools.
source: Metazoan opsins are light-activated GPCRs that have been repurposed as optogenetic tools (Airan et al., 2009; Bailes et al., 2012; Karunarathne et al., 2013; Oh et al., 2010; Siuda et al., 2015), albeit with limitations.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Opsins tend to desensitize after activation due to receptor internalization and/or exhaustion of their chromophore, retinal.
source: For example, opsins tend to desensitize after activation due to receptor internalization and/or exhaustion of their chromophore, retinal (Airan et al., 2009; Bailes et al., 2012; Siuda et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Exogenous supplementation of retinal is required in many experimental settings because this chromophore is not readily synthesized by most mammalian cell types or by many organisms.
source: Exogenous supplementation of retinal, which is not always feasible, is required in many experimental settings because this chomophore is not readily synthesized by most mammalian cell types or by many organisms.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about retinal synthesis in different organisms.

claim: LOV2 uses ubiquitously abundant FMN as the chromophore and does not desensitize.
source: LOV2 uses ubiquitously abundant FMN as the chromophore and does not desensitize.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about LOV2 domain properties.

claim: LOV2 is small (~17 KDa) and expresses easily as a soluble globular protein in different systems.
source: It is small (~17 KDa) and expresses easily as a soluble globular protein in different systems (Lungu et al., 2012; Strickland et al., 2012; Zayner et al., 2013), making it experimentally tractable, easily customizable, and widely applicable.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The GBA motif is a short sequence (~25 amino acids) from the protein GIV that is sufficient to activate heterotrimeric G-protein signaling.
source: We envisioned the design of a genetically-encoded photoswitchable activator of heterotrimeric G-proteins by fusing a short sequence (~25 amino acids) from the protein GIV (a.k.a. Girdin) called the Gα-Binding-and-Activating (GBA) motif to the C-terminus of LOV2 (Figure 1A, left). GBA motifs are evolutionarily conserved sequences found in various cytoplasmic, non-GPCR proteins that are sufficient to activate heterotrimeric G-protein signaling (DiGiacomo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The GBA motif becomes uncaged and binds G-proteins when the C-terminal Jα-helix of LOV2 becomes disordered upon illumination.
source: We reasoned that the GBA motif would be 'uncaged' and bind G-proteins when the C-terminal Jα-helix of LOV2 becomes disordered upon illumination (Harper et al., 2003; Figure 1A, right).
evidence: This is the design principle based on known LOV2 properties (citation) and demonstrated in Figure 1A.

claim: LOV2GIV (L) binds Gαi3 better than LOV2GIV (D).
source: LOV2GIV (L) binds Gαi3 better than LOV2GIV (D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with protein binding experiments.

claim: The first LOV2GIV prototype bound Gαi3 in the lit conformation only ~3 times more than in the dark conformation.
source: Our first LOV2GIV prototype had a suboptimal dynamic range, as it bound the G-protein Gαi3 in the lit conformation only ~3 times more than in the dark conformation (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is quantified from the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Gαi3-binding residues of the GIV GBA motif (L1682, F1685, L1686) are relatively accessible within the dark conformation of LOV2GIV.
source: Based on a structural homology model of LOV2GIV (Figure 1C), we reasoned that it could be due to the relatively high accessibility of Gαi3-binding residues of the GIV GBA motif (L1682, F1685, L1686) within the dark conformation of LOV2GIV.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural homology model shown in Figure 1C.

claim: LOV2GIVe variant 'e' displays greatly diminished Gαi3 binding compared to LOV2GIV wt in the dark conformation.
source: LOV2GIV (D) variant 'e' displays greatly diminished Gαi3 binding compared to LOV2GIV (D) wt.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D with protein binding experiments.

claim: The lit conformation of LOV2GIVe displayed robust Gαi3 binding.
source: In contrast, the lit conformation of LOV2GIVe displayed robust Gαi3 binding, thereby confirming an improved dynamic range compared to the LOV2GIV prototype (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F with protein binding experiments.

claim: LOV2GIVe has an improved dynamic range compared to the LOV2GIV prototype.
source: In contrast, the lit conformation of LOV2GIVe displayed robust Gαi3 binding, thereby confirming an improved dynamic range compared to the LOV2GIV prototype (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing binding data in Figure 1F.

claim: Mutation of GIV's F1685 to alanine results in greatly diminished binding of Gαi3 to the lit conformation of LOV2GIVe.
source: Mutation of GIV's F1685 to alanine, a replacement known to preclude G-protein binding (de Opakua et al., 2017; Garcia-Marcos et al., 2009), resulted in greatly diminished binding of Gαi3 to the lit conformation of LOV2GIVe (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and supported by citations.

claim: The affinity of Gαi3 for the dark conformation of LOV2GIVe is orders of magnitude weaker than for the lit conformation.
source: Concentration-dependent binding curves revealed that the affinity of Gαi3 for the dark conformation of LOV2GIVe is orders of magnitude weaker than for the lit conformation (Figure 2A), which had an equilibrium dissociation constant (KD) similar to that previously reported for the GIV-Gαi3 interaction (DiGiacomo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A with concentration-dependent binding curves.

claim: The lit conformation of LOV2GIVe has an equilibrium dissociation constant (KD) for Gαi3 similar to that previously reported for the GIV-Gαi3 interaction.
source: Concentration-dependent binding curves revealed that the affinity of Gαi3 for the dark conformation of LOV2GIVe is orders of magnitude weaker than for the lit conformation (Figure 2A), which had an equilibrium dissociation constant (KD) similar to that previously reported for the GIV-Gαi3 interaction (DiGiacomo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2A and compared to published data via citation.

claim: LOV2GIVe retains the same G-protein specificity as GIV.
source: We also found that LOV2GIVe retains the same G-protein specificity as GIV.
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 2B with binding experiments to different G-proteins.

claim: LOV2GIVe binds robustly only to members of the Gi/o family among the four families of Gα proteins.
source: Much like GIV (Garcia-Marcos et al., 2010; Marivin et al., 2020), LOV2GIVe bound robustly only to members of the Gi/o family among the four families of Gα proteins (Gi/o, Gs, Gq/11,and G12/13), and could discriminate within the Gi/o family by binding to Gαi1, Gαi2 and Gαi3 but not to Gαo (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and compared to published data on GIV via citations.

claim: LOV2GIVe can discriminate within the Gi/o family by binding to Gαi1, Gαi2 and Gαi3 but not to Gαo.
source: Much like GIV (Garcia-Marcos et al., 2010; Marivin et al., 2020), LOV2GIVe bound robustly only to members of the Gi/o family among the four families of Gα proteins (Gi/o, Gs, Gq/11,and G12/13), and could discriminate within the Gi/o family by binding to Gαi1, Gαi2 and Gαi3 but not to Gαo (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B with binding experiments.

claim: Under steady-state conditions, nucleotide exchange is rate limiting for Gαi proteins because GTP hydrolysis occurs orders of magnitude faster than GTP loading.
source: Under steady-state conditions, nucleotide exchange is rate limiting because GTP hydrolysis occurs orders of magnitude faster than GTP loading for Gαi proteins (Mukhopadhyay and Ross, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Steady-state GTP hydrolysis can report changes in the rate of nucleotide exchange on Gαi.
source: Thus, steady-state GTP hydrolysis can report changes in the rate of nucleotide exchange on Gαi, which we have previously validated for GIV and other related non-receptor GEFs (Aznar et al., 2015; Coleman et al., 2016; Garcia-Marcos et al., 2010; Garcia-Marcos et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LOV2GIVe in the lit, but not the dark, conformation led to a dose-dependent increase of Gαi3 activity.
source: We found that LOV2GIVe in the lit, but not the dark, conformation led to a dose-dependent increase of Gαi3 activity (Figure 2C), which was comparable to that previously shown for GIV (Garcia-Marcos et al., 2009).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C with steady-state GTPase activity assays.

claim: LOV2GIVe in the lit conformation promoted nucleotide exchange on Gαi3.
source: Using a GTPγS binding assay that measures nucleotide exchange more directly, we also found that LOV2GIVe in the lit conformation promoted nucleotide exchange on Gαi3, an effect that was impaired upon introduction of the F1685A (FA) mutation that reduces G-protein binding or when using the dark-mimicking mutant (D) of LOV2GIVe (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 with GTPγS binding assays.

claim: The F1685A (FA) mutation impairs LOV2GIVe's ability to promote nucleotide exchange on Gαi3.
source: Using a GTPγS binding assay that measures nucleotide exchange more directly, we also found that LOV2GIVe in the lit conformation promoted nucleotide exchange on Gαi3, an effect that was impaired upon introduction of the F1685A (FA) mutation that reduces G-protein binding or when using the dark-mimicking mutant (D) of LOV2GIVe (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 with GTPγS binding assays.

claim: LOV2GIVe recapitulates the G-protein activating properties of GIV in vitro.
source: These findings indicate that LOV2GIVe recapitulates the G-protein activating properties of GIV in vitro, and that these are effectively suppressed for the dark conformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the GTPase and GTPγS binding assay results shown in Figures 2C and 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The G-protein activating properties of LOV2GIVe are effectively suppressed for the dark conformation.
source: These findings indicate that LOV2GIVe recapitulates the G-protein activating properties of GIV in vitro, and that these are effectively suppressed for the dark conformation.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the lack of activity of the dark conformation in Figures 2C and 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Expression of LOV2GIVe (L) fused to a membrane-targeting sequence (mLOV2GIVe) led to a very strong induction of β-galactosidase activity in yeast.
source: Expressing LOV2GIVe (L) fused to a membrane-targeting sequence (mLOV2GIVe) led to a very strong induction of β-galactosidase activity, which was not recapitulated by expression of mLOV2GIVe (D) or wt (Figure 3A, right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A with β-galactosidase activity measurements in yeast.

claim: Expression of mLOV2GIVe (D) or wt did not induce strong β-galactosidase activity in yeast.
source: Expressing LOV2GIVe (L) fused to a membrane-targeting sequence (mLOV2GIVe) led to a very strong induction of β-galactosidase activity, which was not recapitulated by expression of mLOV2GIVe (D) or wt (Figure 3A, right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A with β-galactosidase activity measurements in yeast.

claim: LOV2GIVe-mediated activation levels are comparable to those previously reported for the endogenous pathway in response to GPCR activation by mating pheromone.
source: LOV2GIVe-mediated activation levels (several hundred-fold over basal) are comparable to those previously reported for the endogenous pathway in response to GPCR activation by mating pheromone (Hoffman et al., 2002; Lambert et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 3A and compared to published literature via citations.

claim: Expression of mLOV2GIVe (L), but not (D), led to an increase of BRET proportional to the amount of plasmid transfected in mammalian cells.
source: Expression of mLOV2GIVe (L), but not (D), led to an increase of BRET proportional to the amount of plasmid transfected (Figure 3B, right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B with BRET measurements in HEK293T cells.

claim: At the highest amount tested, mLOV2GIVe (L) caused a BRET increase comparable to that observed upon maximal stimulation of the M4 muscarinic receptor.
source: At the highest amount tested, mLOV2GIVe (L) caused a BRET increase comparable to that observed upon maximal stimulation of the M4 muscarinic receptor, a Gi-activating GPCR (Figure 3B, right, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 3B and 3—figure supplement 1 with BRET measurements.

claim: Introducing the F1685A (FA) mutation in mLOV2GIVe (L) abolished its ability to induce a BRET increase.
source: Introducing a mutation that precludes G-protein activation by GIV's GBA motif (F1685A (FA), [Garcia-Marcos et al., 2009]), in mLOV2GIVe (L) also abolished its ability to induce a BRET increase (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 with BRET measurements.

claim: Acute activation of Gi proteins leads to inhibition of adenylyl cyclase activity.
source: Acute activation of Gi proteins leads to inhibition of adenylyl cyclase activity, but prolonged Gi activation leads to the opposite effect— it sensitizes adenylyl cyclases to subsequent activating inputs, such as the stimulation of a Gs-linked GPCR, leading to the potentiation of cAMP production (Brust et al., 2015; Watts and Neve, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Prolonged Gi activation sensitizes adenylyl cyclases to subsequent activating inputs, leading to the potentiation of cAMP production.
source: Acute activation of Gi proteins leads to inhibition of adenylyl cyclase activity, but prolonged Gi activation leads to the opposite effect— it sensitizes adenylyl cyclases to subsequent activating inputs, such as the stimulation of a Gs-linked GPCR, leading to the potentiation of cAMP production (Brust et al., 2015; Watts and Neve, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Expression of LOV2GIVe (L) leads to a potentiation of the cAMP response induced by the β-adrenergic agonist isoproterenol.
source: We found that expression of LOV2GIVe (L) leads to a potentiation of the cAMP response induced by the β-adrenergic agonist isoproterenol, suggesting prolonged activation of Gi proteins in cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 with cAMP measurements.

claim: The magnitude of the cAMP potentiation by LOV2GIVe (L) (~2 fold) is comparable to that reported for many Gi-activating GPCRs.
source: The magnitude of the potentiation (~2 fold) is comparable to that reported for many Gi-activating GPCRs (Watts and Neve, 2005).
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 and compared to published literature via citation.

claim: Expression of LOV2GIVe (L) bearing the F1685A (FA) mutation failed to recapitulate the potentiation of the cAMP response elicited by LOV2GIV (L).
source: In contrast, expression of similar amounts of LOV2GIVe (L) bearing the F1685A (FA) mutation or of LOV2GIVe (D), which do not bind or activate Gαi, failed to recapitulate the potentiation of the cAMP response elicited by LOV2GIV (L) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), further supporting the involvement of Gαi activation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 with cAMP measurements.

claim: Expression of LOV2GIVe (D) failed to recapitulate the potentiation of the cAMP response elicited by LOV2GIV (L).
source: In contrast, expression of similar amounts of LOV2GIVe (L) bearing the F1685A (FA) mutation or of LOV2GIVe (D), which do not bind or activate Gαi, failed to recapitulate the potentiation of the cAMP response elicited by LOV2GIV (L) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), further supporting the involvement of Gαi activation.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3 with cAMP measurements.

claim: The lit conformation of LOV2GIVe activates G-protein signaling in different cell types.
source: Taken together, our results indicate that the lit conformation of LOV2GIVe activates G-protein signaling in different cell types.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results shown in Figure 3 across yeast and mammalian cells.

claim: In HEK293T cells expressing mLOV2GIVe wt, a single short light pulse resulted in a spike of G-protein activation that decayed at a rate similar to that reported for the transition from lit to dark conformation of LOV2 (T1/2 ~1 min).
source: We found that, in HEK293T cells expressing mLOV2GIVe wt, a single short light pulse resulted in a spike of G-protein activation that decayed at a rate similar to that reported for the transition from lit to dark conformation of LOV2 (T1/2 ~1 min) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A with kinetic BRET measurements and compared to known LOV2 properties.

claim: The light-induced G-protein activation response was not recapitulated by a mLOV2GIVe construct bearing the GEF-deficient FA mutation.
source: This response was not recapitulated by a mLOV2GIVe construct bearing the GEF-deficient FA mutation (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A with kinetic BRET measurements.

claim: Yeast cells expressing mLOV2GIVe wt grew in the absence of histidine only when exposed to blue light.
source: Yeast cells expressing mLOV2GIVe wt grew in the absence of histidine only when exposed to blue light (Figure 4B, right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B with spot growth assays.

claim: Cells expressing the light-insensitive mLOV2GIVe (D) construct failed to grow under illumination conditions.
source: This effect was specifically caused by light-dependent activation of mLOV2GIVe wt because cells expressing the light-insensitive mLOV2GIVe (D) construct failed to grow under the same illumination conditions, whereas mLOV2GIVe (L) grew the same regardless of illumination conditions (Figure 4B, right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B with spot growth assays.

claim: mLOV2GIVe (L) grew the same regardless of illumination conditions.
source: This effect was specifically caused by light-dependent activation of mLOV2GIVe wt because cells expressing the light-insensitive mLOV2GIVe (D) construct failed to grow under the same illumination conditions, whereas mLOV2GIVe (L) grew the same regardless of illumination conditions (Figure 4B, right).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B with spot growth assays.

claim: mLOV2GIVe activates G-protein signaling in cells upon blue light illumination.
source: Taken together, these results show that mLOV2GIVe activates G-protein signaling in cells upon blue light illumination.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined results shown in Figure 4.

claim: LOV2GIVe requires targeting to membranes where the substrate G-protein localizes.
source: Given that our results indicate that LOV2GIVe requires targeting to membranes where the substrate G-protein localizes (Figure 3A), it would be possible in the future to target it to different membranous organelles to trigger Gi activation in specific subcellular compartments.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 3A showing that membrane-targeted LOV2GIVe is more effective than cytosolic LOV2GIVe.

claim: Recent evidence suggests that opioid receptors can activate Gi proteins in different subcellular compartments.
source: For example, recent evidence suggests that opiod receptors can activate Gi proteins in different subcellular compartments (Stoeber et al., 2018), but it has not been possible to control GPCR activation in specific subcellular compartments to address the consequences of spatially encoded signals.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: It has not been possible to control GPCR activation in specific subcellular compartments to address the consequences of spatially encoded signals.
source: For example, recent evidence suggests that opiod receptors can activate Gi proteins in different subcellular compartments (Stoeber et al., 2018), but it has not been possible to control GPCR activation in specific subcellular compartments to address the consequences of spatially encoded signals.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of current limitations in the field.

claim: Gi proteins are critical mediators of inhibitory neuromodulation.
source: LOV2GIVe could also be useful for neurobiogical applications because Gi proteins are critical mediator of inhibitory neuromodulation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Gi protein function.

claim: LOV2GIVe can activate G-protein signaling in cellular systems where there is not sufficient synthesis of retinal to support opsin-based activation, like in the yeast S. cerevisiae.
source: Our results also support that LOV2GIVe can activate G-protein signaling even in cellular systems where there is not sufficient synthesis of retinal to support opsin-based activation, like in the yeast S. cerevisiae (Scott et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the yeast experiments in Figures 3A and 4B, and supported by a citation about retinal synthesis in yeast.

claim: Optogenetic approaches allow for the rapid and accurate temporal control of both activation and deactivation compared to chemogenetics with DREADDs.
source: A general advantage of optogenetic approaches over other synthetic biology approaches to activate G-proteins like chemogenetics with Designer Receptors Exclusively Activated by Designer Drugs (DREADDs) (Urban and Roth, 2015) is that they allow for the rapid and accurate temporal control of both activation and deactivation.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about optogenetics and chemogenetics, supported by a citation.

claim: A limitation of LOV2GIVe is that it only acts on one subset of heterotrimeric G-proteins, those containing Gαi subunits.
source: A limitation of LOV2GIVe is that it only acts on one subset of heterotrimeric G-proteins, those containing Gαi subunits.
evidence: This is inferred from the specificity data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Gi proteins control processes as diverse as inhibitory neuromodulation, opioid action, or heart rate.
source: Nevertheless, potential applications are still broad, as Gi proteins control processes as diverse as inhibitory neuromodulation, opioid action, or heart rate, among many others.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about Gi protein function.

claim: GIV requires membrane localization to efficiently activate G-proteins.
source: We reasoned that this could be due to the subcellular localization of the construct, presumed to be cytosolic in the absence of any targeting sequence, because we have previously shown that GIV requires membrane localization to efficiently activate G-proteins (Parag-Sharma et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The C450S mutation mimics the dark conformation of LOV2.
source: To facilitate the biochemical characterization of LOV2GIV, we initially used two well-validated mutants that mimic either the dark (D) or the lit (L) conformation of LOV2 (Harper et al., 2004; Harper et al., 2003; Zimmerman et al., 2016; Figure 1A, right), with the intent of subsequently validating the G-protein regulatory activity of LOV2GIVe in cells using light.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The I539E mutation mimics the lit conformation of LOV2.
source: To facilitate the biochemical characterization of LOV2GIV, we initially used two well-validated mutants that mimic either the dark (D) or the lit (L) conformation of LOV2 (Harper et al., 2004; Harper et al., 2003; Zimmerman et al., 2016; Figure 1A, right), with the intent of subsequently validating the G-protein regulatory activity of LOV2GIVe in cells using light.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Amino acids required for G-protein binding are less accessible in LOV2GIVe than in the LOV2GIV prototype.
source: Consistent with this, a structure homology model of LOV2GIVe showed that amino acids required for G-protein binding are less accessible than in the LOV2GIV prototype (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural homology model shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The F1685A mutation is known to preclude G-protein binding.
source: Mutation of GIV's F1685 to alanine, a replacement known to preclude G-protein binding (de Opakua et al., 2017; Garcia-Marcos et al., 2009), resulted in greatly diminished binding of Gαi3 to the lit conformation of LOV2GIVe (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The L514K and L531E mutations reduce the spurious unwinding of the Jα helix in the dark conformation of LOV2.
source: Two previously described LOV2 mutations (L514K and L531E) that reduce the spurious unwinding of the Jα helix in the dark conformation (Lungu et al., 2012; Zimmerman et al., 2016) were introduced in this construct.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LOV2 is derived from Avena sativa.
source: Here we leveraged the light-sensitive LOV2 domain of Avena sativa (Harper et al., 2003) to develop an optogenetic activator of heterotrimeric G-proteins not based on opsins.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: GBA motifs are evolutionarily conserved sequences found in various cytoplasmic, non-GPCR proteins.
source: GBA motifs are evolutionarily conserved sequences found in various cytoplasmic, non-GPCR proteins that are sufficient to activate heterotrimeric G-protein signaling (DiGiacomo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: The C-terminal Jα-helix of LOV2 becomes disordered upon illumination.
source: We reasoned that the GBA motif would be 'uncaged' and bind G-proteins when the C-terminal Jα-helix of LOV2 becomes disordered upon illumination (Harper et al., 2003; Figure 1A, right).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Fusion of the GBA motif at positions of the Jα helix more proximal to the core of the LOV2 domain tended to lower G-protein binding.
source: In agreement with this idea, fusion of the GBA motif at positions of the Jα helix more proximal to the core of the LOV2 domain tended to lower G-protein binding, including one variant ('e', henceforth referred to as LOV2GIVe) in which binding to the dark conformation was almost undetectable (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D with protein binding experiments.

claim: Binding to the dark conformation was almost undetectable for LOV2GIVe variant 'e'.
source: In agreement with this idea, fusion of the GBA motif at positions of the Jα helix more proximal to the core of the LOV2 domain tended to lower G-protein binding, including one variant ('e', henceforth referred to as LOV2GIVe) in which binding to the dark conformation was almost undetectable (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D with protein binding experiments.

claim: The GEF activity of LOV2GIVe (L) is comparable to that previously shown for GIV.
source: We found that LOV2GIVe in the lit, but not the dark, conformation led to a dose-dependent increase of Gαi3 activity (Figure 2C), which was comparable to that previously shown for GIV (Garcia-Marcos et al., 2009).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and compared to published data via citation.

claim: The humanized yeast strain CY7967 has the gene encoding the pheromone responsive GPCR (STE3) deleted.
source: The main features of this strain are that the gene encoding only pheromone responsive GPCR (STE3) is deleted, the endogenous Gα-subunit Gpa1 is replaced by a chimeric Gpa1(1-41)-human Gαi3 (36-354) and the gene encoding the cell cycle arrest-inducing protein Far1 is deleted.
evidence: This describes the features of the yeast strain used in the experiments.

claim: In the humanized yeast strain CY7967, the endogenous Gα-subunit Gpa1 is replaced by a chimeric Gpa1(1-41)-human Gαi3 (36-354).
source: The main features of this strain are that the gene encoding only pheromone responsive GPCR (STE3) is deleted, the endogenous Gα-subunit Gpa1 is replaced by a chimeric Gpa1(1-41)-human Gαi3 (36-354) and the gene encoding the cell cycle arrest-inducing protein Far1 is deleted.
evidence: This describes the features of the yeast strain used in the experiments.

claim: In the humanized yeast strain CY7967, the gene encoding the cell cycle arrest-inducing protein Far1 is deleted.
source: The main features of this strain are that the gene encoding only pheromone responsive GPCR (STE3) is deleted, the endogenous Gα-subunit Gpa1 is replaced by a chimeric Gpa1(1-41)-human Gαi3 (36-354) and the gene encoding the cell cycle arrest-inducing protein Far1 is deleted.
evidence: This describes the features of the yeast strain used in the experiments.

claim: In the humanized yeast strain, the pheromone response pathway can be upregulated by the ectopic expression of activators of human Gαi3 and does not result in cell cycle arrest.
source: In this strain, the pheromone response pathway can be upregulated by the ectopic expression of activators of human Gαi3 and does not result in the cell cycle arrest that occurs in the native pheromone response (Cismowski et al., 2002; Cismowski et al., 1999; Maziarz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: LOV2GIVe could be targeted to different membranous organelles to trigger Gi activation in specific subcellular compartments.
source: Given that our results indicate that LOV2GIVe requires targeting to membranes where the substrate G-protein localizes (Figure 3A), it would be possible in the future to target it to different membranous organelles to trigger Gi activation in specific subcellular compartments.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future applications based on the observed membrane-targeting requirement.

claim: LOV2GIVe could be leveraged to assess the different impact of inhibitory modulation at pre- or post-synaptic sites.
source: Combined with the potential for subcellular compartmentalization, LOV2GIVe could be leveraged to assess the different impact of inhibitory modulation at pre- or post-synaptic sites.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications.

claim: LOV2GIVe could open the application of optogenetic Gi activation to organisms or experimental settings in which the lack of external supplementation of retinal is detrimental.
source: This could open the application of optogenetic Gi activation to organisms or experimental settings in which the lack of external supplementation of retinal is detrimental, such those required prolonged and/or repeated stimulation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications based on the FMN chromophore advantage.

claim: LOV2GIVe could be used to investigate Gi signaling processes over a broad temporal scale, including intermittent or pulsatile activation.
source: Thus, LOV2GIVe could be used to investigate Gi signaling processes over a broad temporal scale, also including intermittent or pulsatile activation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential future applications based on the optogenetic control properties.

claim: Opsins are relatively large, post-translationally modified transmembrane proteins, which makes them inherently difficult to modify for optimization and/or customization for specific applications.
source: Also, opsins are relatively large, post-translationally modified transmembrane proteins, which makes them inherently difficult to modify for optimization and/or customization for specific applications.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about opsin properties.

claim: The M4 muscarinic receptor is a Gi-activating GPCR.
source: At the highest amount tested, mLOV2GIVe (L) caused a BRET increase comparable to that observed upon maximal stimulation of the M4 muscarinic receptor, a Gi-activating GPCR (Figure 3B, right, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about the M4 receptor.

claim: Adenylyl cyclases are classical effectors of GTP-bound Gαi subunits.
source: As an alternative readout of G-protein regulation by LOV2GIVe, we measured cAMP levels in cells because the enzymes that produce this second messenger, adenylyl cyclases, are classical effectors of GTP-bound Gαi subunits.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about adenylyl cyclase regulation.

claim: The decay rate of G-protein activation after a light pulse is similar to that reported for the transition from lit to dark conformation of LOV2 (T1/2 ~1 min).
source: We found that, in HEK293T cells expressing mLOV2GIVe wt, a single short light pulse resulted in a spike of G-protein activation that decayed at a rate similar to that reported for the transition from lit to dark conformation of LOV2 (T1/2 ~1 min) (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A and compared to known LOV2 properties.
